passages.text: SPLEEN, in anatomy, a soft, spongy viscus of a livid colour, situated in the left side of the belly, between the stomach and the ribs.
The use of the spleen is not yet known, and anatomists have offered many conjectures concerning it.
The ancients made the spleen the seat of melancholy, and some of them of laughter; whence the word spleen is still used for ill humour.
Dogs from which the spleen has been cut out have lived many years after, and have been in good health; so that it cannot be absolutely necessary to life.
Some suppose that the blood, moving slowly through the spleen, is there prepared for the better secretion of the bile in the liver, to which it goes by the splenic vein.
Others imagine that it sends a juice to the stomach by the short vessels, to sharpen the appetite and assist digestion.
In some fevers, particularly in the intermittent, the spleen swells to a great size and becomes hard; this the common people call the ague-cake.
The spleen is an organ found in almost all vertebrates. In humans it lies in the upper left part of the abdomen. It works mainly as a filter for the blood.
The spleen removes old and damaged red blood cells. Their iron is recycled, and their hemoglobin is broken down to bilirubin, which travels to the liver and leaves the body in the bile.
The spleen is part of the immune system. Its white pulp holds lymphocytes and helps the body fight bacteria, especially bacteria with a capsule.
The spleen holds a reserve of blood cells. In some animals, such as horses, it can release many red blood cells into the blood during exertion.
People can live without a spleen. After its removal, called splenectomy, they have a higher risk of serious infections, so vaccination is advised.
An enlarged spleen, called splenomegaly, has many causes, including infections such as malaria and infectious mononucleosis.
In the humoral medicine of ancient Greece the spleen was linked to black bile and melancholy. In English the word spleen came to mean bad temper.

reasons: Rare terms appear in both: melancholy, splenic vein, enlarged spleen in fevers.
Splenectomy scores well but covers only the removal of the organ.

alignments.label: Use of the spleen

britannica.quote: The use of the spleen is not yet known

wikipedia.quote: It works mainly as a filter for the blood

alignments.note: Change in knowledge. The statement was fair in 1797. Today the main uses are known.

alignments.label: Seat of melancholy

britannica.quote: The ancients made the spleen the seat of melancholy

wikipedia.quote: linked to black bile and melancholy

alignments.note: Both report the old belief and its trace in the word spleen. Neither endorses it.

alignments.label: Life without a spleen

britannica.quote: it cannot be absolutely necessary to life

wikipedia.quote: People can live without a spleen

alignments.note: Same conclusion. Wikipedia adds that the risk of serious infection goes up.

alignments.label: Link to the bile

britannica.quote: is there prepared for the better secretion of the bile in the liver

wikipedia.quote: travels to the liver and leaves the body in the bile

alignments.note: Inference: the old guess points in a real direction. The spleen breaks down old red cells, and their waste goes to the liver and into the bile.

alignments.label: Juice for the stomach

britannica.quote: it sends a juice to the stomach by the short vessels

alignments.note: The short vessels carry blood, not a digestive juice. Wikipedia does not mention this old idea.

alignments.label: Swelling in fevers

britannica.quote: the spleen swells to a great size and becomes hard

alignments.note: Same observation. The intermittent fever of 1797 is mostly malaria, which Wikipedia names as a cause.

alignments.label: Immune role

wikipedia.quote: The spleen is part of the immune system

alignments.note: The 1797 entry knows nothing of the spleen's part in fighting infection.

wikipedia.quote: holds a reserve of blood cells

suggestedQuestions: What did the 1797 entry know about the use of the spleen?
Can you live without a spleen?

What did the 1797 entry know about the u.answer: It said the use was not yet known [B2]. It listed guesses: preparing blood for the bile [B5] and sending a juice to the stomach [B6]. Wikipedia says the spleen filters the blood [W1], removes old red cells [W2] and is part of the immune system [W3].

Can you live without a spleen?.answer: The 1797 entry says dogs lived many years after the spleen was cut out [B4]. Wikipedia agrees that people can live without it, but notes a higher risk of serious infections [W5].
